title: Unit 3 Check: Forces, Plants, and Body Systems
description: 13 questions on Unit 3 (lessons 16.01 to 19.02): mass and forces, where plants get their materials, scientific arguments, food energy from the sun, food chain models, and body systems working together. Read each question carefully. Some questions have a small data table.

questions.q: A soccer ball and a bowling ball sit on the floor. You give each one the same gentle kick. What happens?
opts: The soccer ball rolls farther, because it has less mass
The bowling ball rolls farther, because heavy things keep going
They roll the same distance, because the kicks were the same
Neither one moves, because the forces are balanced
questions.why: The same force has a bigger effect on an object with less mass.

questions.q: Two dogs pull on opposite ends of a rope toy. The toy slowly moves toward the bigger dog. What does this show?
opts: The forces are balanced
The forces are unbalanced, and the bigger dog pulls with more force
No forces are acting on the toy
The smaller dog is pulling harder
questions.why: When opposite forces are not equal, the object moves toward the bigger force.

questions.q:
A student flicked two objects with the same push, three times each, and measured how far they slid.

ObjectTrial 1Trial 2Trial 3
Tennis ball (light)42 cm38 cm40 cm
Hardcover book (heavy)7 cm5 cm6 cm

Which conclusion does this data support?
opts: The book moved less because it was pushed with less force
Mass does not change how far an object moves
The same push moved the light object much farther, so more mass means less motion from the same force
The heavy object moved farther on average
questions.why: The pushes were the same, and the light ball went about 40 cm while the book went about 6 cm.

questions.from: 16.02, Part 1 (Stop and Think: why the same push)
questions.q: In the mass test, why should both objects get the same push?
opts: So both objects stop in the same place
So the heavy object can win
It does not matter how hard you push each one
So the only thing that changes is the mass, and the test is fair
questions.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Then any difference in the results comes from the mass.

questions.from: 17.01, Parts 2 and 4 (air and water build the plant)
questions.q: A pumpkin vine grows from one small seed into a plant with 10 kilograms of leaves, stems, and pumpkins. The soil in its pot barely changes. Where did most of the plant's new mass come from?
opts: Nutrients the roots pulled out of the soil
Carbon dioxide from the air, and water
Sunlight that turned into solid material
The fertilizer that was added to the pot
questions.why: Plants build their bodies mostly from carbon dioxide and water. Sunlight gives the energy, but it is not the material.

questions.q: True or false: Fertilizer is the food that plants eat to build their bodies.
questions.why: Fertilizer adds small amounts of nutrients, minerals like nitrogen, that help plants grow. Plants make their own food using light, air, and water.

questions.from: 17.02, Part 1 (three parts of a scientific argument)
questions.q: Match each sentence to the part of a scientific argument it is.
pairs: Plants get most of their mass from air and water.
The willow tree gained 164 pounds while the soil lost only 2 ounces.
The soil barely changed, so the tree's new mass must have come from somewhere else, like the air and water.
questions.why: A claim says what is true, evidence is the data, and reasoning explains how the data proves the claim.

questions.q:
A plant was sealed in a clear jar with a carbon dioxide meter.

TimeLampCarbon dioxide in the jar
Starton420
After 2 hourson200
After 4 hoursoff for the last 2 hours230

What does this data show?
opts: The plant took in carbon dioxide all the time, light or dark
The plant took in carbon dioxide while it had light, and stopped when the light was off
The soil soaked up the carbon dioxide
The jar must have had a leak
questions.why: The number fell with the lamp on and crept back up with the lamp off. Light powers the plant's building.

questions.q: Which of these living things can make its own food using energy from sunlight?
opts: A rabbit
An oak tree
A hawk
A grasshopper
questions.why: Plants are producers. They use sunlight to make food. Animals are consumers and must eat.

questions.q: In the food chain model Grass → Rabbit → Fox, what does the arrow from the rabbit to the fox stand for?
opts: The rabbit eats the fox
Energy moves from the rabbit to the fox when the fox eats it
The fox gives energy to the rabbit
The rabbit runs toward the fox
questions.why: Food chain arrows point toward the eater. They show which way the energy flows.

questions.q: Match each organ to its main job.
pairs: Pumps blood to every part of the body
Take in oxygen and push out carbon dioxide
Mashes food and mixes it with juices
Thinks, feels, and sends messages to the body
Filter waste and extra water out of the blood
extra: Holds you up and protects organs
questions.why: Each organ has its own function, and they work as a team.

questions.from: 19.02, Part 4 (the pulse lab) and Part 2 (Keep the gauges up)
questions.q:
A student measured these numbers.

At restAfter 1 minute of jumping jacks
Heartbeats per minute80128
Breaths in 30 seconds814

Which explanation fits this data best?
opts: The heart got tired, so it had to beat faster
The lungs sent air straight to the muscles, so the heart did not matter
The muscles needed more oxygen, so the lungs and the heart sped up together to deliver it
The digestive system sped up the heart
questions.why: Working muscles need more oxygen. The lungs bring it into the blood and the heart pumps that blood to the muscles, so both speed up.

questions.q: In a box-and-arrow model of body systems, what does the arrow from the lungs to the heart and blood carry?
opts: Nutrients
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Signals
questions.why: In the lungs, oxygen moves from the air into the blood. Carbon dioxide goes the other way, out of the blood and out with your breath.
